3.1.m: Now begins the Setumāhātmya, the first [part] in the Brāhmakhaṇḍa. (3.1)

Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Homage to the venerable Veda-Vyāsa.
One should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who wears white garments, is the color of the moon, has four arms,
and has a serene face, for the pacification of all obstacles. (1)
The seers headed by Śaunaka, residing in Naimiṣāraṇya,
were devoted to the eightfold yoga and solely dedicated to the knowledge of Brahman. (1)
Desiring liberation, great-souled, free from possessiveness, expounders of Brahman,
knowers of dharma, free from envy, and committed to the vow of truth, (2)
subdued of senses, subdued of anger, compassionate to all beings,
worshiping eternal Viṣṇu with supreme devotion, (3)
practiced tapas in the greatly meritorious Naimiṣa, which bestows liberation.
Once those great-souled ones held an excellent gathering, (4)
reciting greatly meritorious stories that destroy sins,
and inquiring of one another the means to worldly enjoyment and liberation. (5)
[There were] twenty-six thousand seers of purified soul;

At that moment, the greatly learned disciple of Vyāsa, the great sage,
Sūta, foremost of Purāṇa reciters, arrived at Naimiṣāraṇya. (7)
Seeing that sage arrived, blazing like fire,
the sages headed by Śaunaka worshiped him with water for guests and other offerings. (8)
When that Sūta was comfortably seated on an excellent, auspicious seat,
desiring the welfare of the worlds, they asked him a supreme secret: (9)
“O Sūta, knower of the true nature of dharma and wealth, welcome, O bull among sages!
You have heard the Purāṇas from Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī. (3.1.1.10)
Therefore, O great sage, you know the meaning of all the Purāṇas.

3.1.m: And by what means does the fruit of threefold action become accomplished for a person?
Kindly tell all of this and whatever else [is secret], O Sūta! (13)
For spiritual teachers tell even a secret to an affectionate disciple.”
Thus questioned then by the dwellers of Naimiṣāraṇya, (14)
Sūta began to speak, having first bowed to his guru Vyāsa.
Śrī Sūta said:
“This has been well asked by you, O brahmins, for the benefit of the world. (15)
I shall tell you this secret; listen with respect.
This has not been spoken by me before to anyone, O bulls among sages. (16)
Restraining your minds, O foremost of brahmins, listen with devotion.
There is [a sacred place] named Rāmeśvara, sanctified at Rāmasetu, (17)
the best of all sacred fields and of all sacred fords.
At the mere sight of Rāmasetu, liberation from the ocean of worldly existence is attained; (18)

How, O highly fortunate Sūta, by Rāma of untiring deeds,

The venerable Sūta said:
Indeed, how the bridge was constructed across the abode of Varuṇa by Rāma,

By command of his father, Rāma lived in the Daṇḍaka forest,
accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, collected in mind at Pañcavaṭī.
While that great-souled descendant of Raghu was dwelling there,
his wife was abducted by Rāvaṇa under the pretext of Mārīca, O twice-born.
Searching for his wife in the forest, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha,
went to the bank of the Pampā, filled with grief and bewilderment.
There the son of Daśaratha saw a certain monkey.
Then that descendant of Raghu was questioned by the monkey: 'Who are you?'

Long ago, a sage named Gālava, devoted to Viṣṇu,
on the shore of the southern ocean, not far from Hālāsya...
and near Phullagrāma, in the vicinity of the Kṣīrasaras,
on the bank of the Dharmapuṣkariṇī, he practiced great austerity,
chanting the eternal Brahman for ten thousand yugas, O brahmins.
Endowed with compassion, fasting, truthful, and subduing his senses,
viewing all living beings like himself, free from longing for sense-objects,
intent on the welfare of all beings, self-restrained, and free from all dualities,
for some years he ate withered leaves;
for some time he subsisted on water, and for a few years he fed on air.
In this manner, for five thousand years, that great sage
performed dreadful austerity, difficult even for the gods to perform.
Then, for five thousand years, that foremost of sages,
taking no food, seeing no light, holding his breath, without a fixed abode,
enduring downpours in the rains, lying in water during the winters,
standing amidst the five fires in summer, devoted to meditation on Viṣṇu,
reciting the eight-syllable mantra and meditating in his heart upon Janārdana,
performed austerity—Gālava, the eminent sage of immense splendor.

Formerly, in the peak of Kailāsa, at Hālāsya, the temple of Śiva,

Headed by Vasiṣṭha and Atri, all devotees of Śiva, endowed with great splendor.

Inhabitants of the city of Madhurā, they worshipped the lord of Hālāsya,
The master of beings, the moon-crested consort of Umā, for the sake of liberation.
Once, at that place, a mighty gandharva, the son of Viśvāvasu,
Named Durdama, O lords among brahmins, devoted to gatherings of profligates,
Surrounded by a hundred women, naked in a reservoir of water—
he sportively played with those unclothed young women with delight.
To that sacred ford of the Lord of Hālāsya, Vasiṣṭha, along with other sages,

The auspicious Sūta said:
Having extolled the sacred Cakratīrtha that destroys sin,
I shall tell yet another wonder, O foremost sages! (1)
A Vasu named Vidhūma and the divine woman Alaṃbuṣā,
formerly attained human birth due to a terrible curse from Brahmā. (2)
Having bathed at the supremely holy Cakratīrtha, they were liberated from the curse.
The seers said:
O Sūta, Sūta, highly wise one, expert in the meaning of the Purāṇas! (3)
Because of your wisdom and your being Vyāsa’s pupil, nothing is unknown to you.
For what offense did the four-faced Brahmā in the past curse the Vasu named Vidhūma,
together with Alaṃbuṣā? (4)
Through the terrible curse of Brahmā, whose son and daughter did the two become? (5)
How did the end of the curse come about for the two cursed by Brahmā?
You ought to tell this in detail to us who are full of faith. (6)
The auspicious Sūta said:
Long ago, the lord Brahmā, the self-manifest, four-faced deity,
flanked on both sides by Sāvitrī and Sarasvatī, (7)
attended by the sage Sanātana and the wise Sanaka,
by the one named Sanatkumāra, and by the noble Nārada, (8)
served by Sanandana and other foremost sages,
praised by Indra who is served by hosts of gods, (9)
his lotus-feet praised by the planets headed by the Sun,
surrounded by Siddhas, Sādhyas, Maruts, and Kinnaras, (10)
accompanied by troops of Kimpuruṣas and by the eight Vasus,
and watching again and again the charming dance
along with instrumental music of heavenly courtesans led by Urvaśī,
once held an assembly in the hall in Satyaloka. (12)
Deep as the rumbling of clouds, continuously delighting the people,
the sound of lutes, flutes, and drums spread there. (13)
Cool from the touch of droplets from the rows of Gaṅgā’s waves,

3.1.s: pavamānaḥ sukhasparśo mandaṃ mandaṃ vavau tadā .. 14 ..
3.1.d: पवमानः सुखस्पर्शो मन्दं मन्दं ववौ तदा .. 14 ..
3.1.m: pleasant to the touch, the wind blew very gently at that time. (14)
Then all the celestial women danced in turn.
When the other courtesans were exhausted by the fatigue of dancing, respectfully (15)
the celestial woman Alaṃbuṣā, endowed with beauty and youth,
enchanting everyone, danced in the midst of the assembly. (16)
At that moment, O brahmins, as she was dancing in the assembly,
the wind playfully blew away her undergarment. (17)
When that garment was lifted, the root of her thighs was clearly seen.

3.1.s: tathābhūtāṃ tu tāṃ dṛṣṭvā sarve brahmādayo hriyā .. 19 ..
3.1.d: तथाभूतां तु तां दृष्ट्वा सर्वे ब्रह्मादयो ह्रिया .. 19 ..
3.1.m: Seeing her in such a state, all those beginning with Brahmā, out of bashfulness, (18)
seated in the middle of the assembly, closed their eyes.
The Vasu named Vidhūma, however, afflicted by the arrows of desire, (19)
seeing her alone in Brahmā’s abode, her garment snatched by the wind,
became full of joy with wide-open eyes and hair standing on end. (20)

3.1.s: alaṃbusāyāṃ tasyāṃ tu jātakāmaṃ vilokya tam ..
3.1.d: अलंबुसायां तस्यां तु जातकामं विलोक्य तम् ..
3.1.m: Observing that he was stricken with passion for Alaṃbuṣā,
the four-faced Brahmā cursed that Vasu named Vidhūma: (21)
“Because you have done such a deed, O Vidhūma,
therefore you will attain a human state in the mortal world. (22)

3.1.s: iyaṃ ca devayoṣitte tatra bhāryā bhaviṣyati ..
3.1.d: इयं च देवयोषित्ते तत्र भार्या भविष्यति ..
3.1.m: And this celestial woman shall be your wife there.”

3.1.s: evaṃ sa brahmaṇā śapto vidhūmaḥ khinnamānasaḥ .. 23 ..
3.1.d: एवं स ब्रह्मणा शप्तो विधूमः खिन्नमानसः .. 23 ..
3.1.m: Thus cursed by Brahmā, Vidhūma, distressed in mind, (23)
prostrated before Brahmā and sought to propitiate him.
Vidhūma said:
“O Lord, lover of your devotees! From this terrible curse (24)
I do not deserve this, O Lord of gods; protect me, O ocean of compassion!”
Propitiated in this manner by him, the imperishable Lord of Bhāratī, (25)

3.1.s: kṛpayā parayā yukto vidhūmaṃ prāha sāṃtvayan ..
3.1.d: कृपया परया युक्तो विधूमं प्राह सांत्वयन् ..
3.1.m: filled with supreme mercy, spoke consolingly to Vidhūma.
Brahmā said:

3.1.s: tvayi śāpo'pyayaṃ datto na cāsatyaṃ bravīmyaham .. 26 ..
3.1.d: त्वयि शापोऽप्ययं दत्तो न चासत्यं ब्रवीम्यहम् .. 26 ..
3.1.m: “Although this curse has been laid upon you, and I do not speak falsely, (26)
I shall now fix an end to this curse of yours.
"Having fallen into mortal existence together with this Alaṃbuṣā,

3.1.s: tatra bhūtvā mahārājaḥ śāsayitvā ciraṃ mahīm ..
3.1.d: तत्र भूत्वा महाराजः शासयित्वा चिरं महीम् ..
3.1.m: having become a great king there and having ruled the earth for a long time,
having begotten upon her a peerless son who will be king,
and having consecrated him on the throne, he who is expert in protecting the kingdom,
then, for the pacification of this curse, on the shore of the southern ocean,
at the most exalted Cakratīrtha situated near Phullagrāma,

3.1.s: anayā bhāryayā sārddhaṃ yadā snānaṃ kariṣyasi ..
3.1.d: अनया भार्यया सार्द्धं यदा स्नानं करिष्यसि ..
3.1.m: when you perform ritual ablution along with this wife,
then you, shedding human existence like a snake sheds its worn-out skin,

3.1.s: visṛjya bhāryayā sārddhaṃ svaṃ lokaṃ pratipatsyase ..
3.1.d: विसृज्य भार्यया सार्द्धं स्वं लोकं प्रतिपत्स्यसे ..
3.1.m: together with your wife, will attain your own realm.

3.1.s: cakratīrthe vinā snānaṃ na naśyecchāpa īdṛśaḥ..31..
3.1.d: चक्रतीर्थे विना स्नानं न नश्येच्छाप ईदृशः..31..
3.1.m: Without ritual ablution at Cakratīrtha, such a curse cannot be destroyed."
Hearing these words of Brahmā, Vidhūma was not greatly pleased.
Taking leave of the four-faced [god], he swiftly entered his own abode.
There he reflected: "When I go into mortality,

3.1.s: ko vā pitā bhavedbhūmau kā vā mātā bhaviṣyati..33..
3.1.d: को वा पिता भवेद्भूमौ का वा माता भविष्यति..33..
3.1.m: who indeed might be my father on earth, and who will be my mother?"
Having reflected thus in many ways, that Vidhūma resolved:
"In the city of Kauśāmbī there is a king renowned as Śatānīka.

3.1.s: asti vīro mahābhāgo bhāryā cāpi pativratā ..
3.1.d: अस्ति वीरो महाभागो भार्या चापि पतिव्रता ..
3.1.m: He is a heroic, highly fortunate man, and his wife is devoted to her husband.
Her name is Viṣṇumatī, beloved to him like Śrī is to Viṣṇu.

3.1.s: tameva pitaraṃ kṛtvā mātaraṃ ca vidhāya tām ..
3.1.d: तमेव पितरं कृत्वा मातरं च विधाय ताम् ..
3.1.m: Making him alone my father, and making her my mother,
I shall be born in the mortal realm through the ripening of my own deeds."

3.1.s: tataḥ sa mālyavantaṃ ca puṣpadaṃtaṃ balotkaṭam..
3.1.d: ततः स माल्यवन्तं च पुष्पदंतं बलोत्कटम्..
3.1.m: Then, having summoned his three servants—Mālyavant, Puṣpadanta,
and the mighty Balotkaṭa—he disclosed this occurrence:
"Servants, listen—blessing be upon you! Because of the great fear of Brahmā's curse,
I will be born as the son of Śatānīka from Viṣṇumatī."

3.1.s: iti śrutvā vaco bhṛtyāstasyā prāṇā bahiścarāḥ ..
3.1.d: इति श्रुत्वा वचो भृत्यास्तस्या प्राणा बहिश्चराः ..
3.1.m: Hearing these words, his servants, who were like his vital breaths wandering outside,
all with faces filled with tears, spoke these words to Vidhūma.
The servants said:

3.1.s: tvadviyogaṃ vayaṃ sarve trayo'pi na sahāmahe ..
3.1.d: त्वद्वियोगं वयं सर्वे त्रयोऽपि न सहामहे ..
3.1.m: "Separation from you, all three of us cannot endure;
therefore, you shall go into human existence together with us.
There is that minister of the royal sage Śatānīka named Yugandhara,
and the general Vipratīka, who marches in the forefront in battle,
and the great brahmin named Vallabha, dear in humorous diversions;
we three shall undoubtedly become their sons.
To you, who have become the son of the royal sage Śatānīka,
we shall render service in various tasks."
To them speaking thus, that Vidhūma spoke [these] words.
Vidhūma said:

3.1.s: jāne'haṃ bhavatāṃ snehaṃ tādṛśaṃ mayya nuttamam .. 44 ..
3.1.d: जानेऽहं भवतां स्नेहं तादृशं मय्य नुत्तमम् .. 44 ..
3.1.m: "I know such peerless affection of yours towards me;
nevertheless, I speak today—hear these beneficial words:
brought about by a terrible curse of Brahmā due to my own wrong deeds,
I alone should undergo this despised human state.
Following this curse is indeed not ordained for you;
therefore, do not set your mind now upon contemptible human existence.
Therefore, until the limit of the curse, let separation from me be endured."
To him who had spoken thus, all of them, led by Mālyavant,
bowing their heads, spoke, entreating him again and again:

3.1.s: rakṣitvā kṛpayā hyasmānmā kuruṣva ca sāhasam ..
3.1.d: रक्षित्वा कृपया ह्यस्मान्मा कुरुष्व च साहसम् ..
3.1.m: "Protect us out of compassion, and do not act rashly!
Are you abandoning all of us today, your guiltless devotees?
Compared to the terrifying separation from you, even contemptible human existence
we deem very worthy, O lord! Therefore, protect us now!"
Thus, he consented to those three servants who were entreating him;
together with those three, he desired to go to Kauśāmbī.
At that very time, however, the enhancer of the lunar dynasty,
born in the lineage of Arjuna, born of Janamejaya,
King Śatānīka was ruling the earth.
Wise, prudent, eloquent, intent on protecting his subjects,
equipped with a fourfold army, having valor as his sole wealth, young—
that great king dwelt in the city of Kauśāmbī.
Knowing the secret of counsel, Yugandhara was his minister,
and Vipratīka was his general, the foremost in battle.
In matters of jest, he had a brahmin friend named Vallabha.

3.1.s: tasya viṣṇumatī nāma viṣṇoḥ śrīriva vallabhā .. 56 ..
3.1.d: तस्य विष्णुमती नाम विष्णोः श्रीरिव वल्लभा .. 56 ..
3.1.m: His beloved [wife] was named Viṣṇumatī, just like Śrī is beloved of Viṣṇu.
Endowed with all virtues, the highly intelligent Śatānīka
did not obtain a son equal to himself from that wife.
Knowing himself to be sonless, he grieved deeply.
Summoning the minister Yugaṃdhara, who was most skilled in counsel,
he deliberated on the matter: “How may I obtain a son?”
Gladdening with his speech the ruler of the earth,
who was afflicted by lack of a son, Yugaṃdhara spoke these words:
Yugaṃdhara said:
“There is a great seer named Śāṇḍilya, truthful in speech and pure,
impartial to foes and friends, self-controlled, devoted to austerity and the study of the Veda.
Approaching that very sage, blazing like fire,
you should humbly ask for a son equal to yourself, O King.

3.1.s: kṛpāvānsa maharṣistu putraṃ te dāsyati dhruvam .. 62 ..
3.1.d: कृपावान्स महर्षिस्तु पुत्रं ते दास्यति ध्रुवम् .. 62 ..
3.1.m: Compassionate as he is, that great seer will surely grant you a son.”
Hearing these words of his, his eyes blossoming with joy,
accompanied by that minister, he went to the hermitage of that sage.
The king bowed down to him as he sat in the hermitage.
Seeing that the king had arrived at the hermitage,

3.1.s: dṛṣṭvā pādyādibhiḥ pūjya svāgataṃ vyājahāra saḥ ..
3.1.d: दृष्ट्वा पाद्यादिभिः पूज्य स्वागतं व्याजहार सः ..
3.1.m: Śāṇḍilya, endowed with great splendor, honored him with water for the feet and other rites, and offered a welcome.
Śāṇḍilya said:
“Śatānīka, for what purpose have you come to my hermitage?
Speak what must be done for you now; I shall do it.”
As the sage was speaking thus, Yugaṃdhara replied to him:
“O venerable one, this king, tormented by lack of a son,
has now come to you for refuge for the sake of a son.
You ought to dispel the sorrow born of his sonlessness.”

3.1.s: iti tasya vacaḥ śrutvā śāṃḍilyo munisattamaḥ ..68..
3.1.d: इति तस्य वचः श्रुत्वा शांडिल्यो मुनिसत्तमः ..68..
3.1.m: Hearing his speech, Śāṇḍilya, the best of sages,
promised the boon of obtaining a son to that king.
That glorious bestower of boons, having respectfully come to Kauśāmbī for the king,
that great sage became the officiating priest in the sacrifice for obtaining a son for him who desired a son.
Then, by the grace of the sage, the king, comparable to Daśaratha,
having performed the sacrifice, obtained a son named Sahasrānīka, just as [Daśaratha obtained] Rāma.
Thus Vidhūma was born from Śatānīka, the best of kings.
Meanwhile, the king's foremost minister and commander-in-chief,
as well as the brahmin jester, obtained sons suitable to their lineages.
The son of Yugaṃdhara was the attendant named Mālyavat,
named Yaugandharāyaṇa, skilled in the sciences of counsel.
Vipratīka's son was indeed Puṣpadanta,
renowned as Rumaṇvat, the crusher of enemy armies.

3.1.s: vallabhasya tadā jajñe tanayo vai balotkaṭaḥ ..
3.1.d: वल्लभस्य तदा जज्ञे तनयो वै बलोत्कटः ..
3.1.m: Then a son of immense strength was born to Vallabha,
known as Vasantaka, skilled in the arts of jest.
Then they all grew up, with the prince leading them.
After they had reached the age of five years,
the celestial courtezan Alambuṣā also [was born] to King Kṛtavarman
in the great city of Ayodhyā as the maiden named Mṛgāvatī.
Thus they, headed by Vidhūma, were born upon the earthly realm.
In the meantime, a mighty [demon] of great strength, having wicked followers,
renowned as Ahidaṃṣṭra, a great Daitya of tremendous might,
joined by an evil-minded ally named Sthūlaśiras,
besieged the city of the gods and oppressed the deities as well.
While the great war between the gods and demons was underway in heaven,
Puraṃdara brought Śatānīka to serve as his ally.

3.1.s: sa yauvarājye tanayaṃ vidhāya vidhinā nṛpaḥ .. 81 ..
3.1.d: स यौवराज्ये तनयं विधाय विधिना नृपः .. 81 ..
3.1.m: Having duly consecrated his son to the position of crown prince,
the king set forth, mounting a chariot, to battle with the sons of Diti.
Brought respectfully by Mātali who had arrived [for him], that archer
made the gods mere spectators and struck down the sons of Diti in battle.

3.1.s: atha daityādhipaḥ so'pi nihataḥ samare divi .. 83 ..
3.1.d: अथ दैत्याधिपः सोऽपि निहतः समरे दिवि .. 83 ..
3.1.m: Then that lord of the Daityas too was slain in battle in heaven.
Then, by the order of Śakra, placing that dead bull among kings
swiftly upon the chariot, Mātali went to Kauśāmbī.
Having brought [the king's body] to the surface of the earth, he presented it to his son.
Then Sahasrānīka also, weeping and deeply distressed,
joined together with the ministers and performed the funeral rites.

3.1.s: mṛtaṃ jñātvā patiṃ rājñī sahaivānumamāra ca .. 86 ..
3.1.d: मृतं ज्ञात्वा पतिं राज्ञी सहैवानुममार च .. 86 ..
3.1.m: Learning that her husband was dead, the queen died alongside him.
When the king, along with his queen, had attained the state of living only in fame,
Śatānīka's son took up the kingdom at the bidding of the ministers.

3.1.s: yugandhare vipratīke vallabhe ca mṛte sati ..
3.1.d: युगन्धरे विप्रतीके वल्लभे च मृते सति ..
3.1.m: When Yugandhara, Vipratīka, and Vallabha had died,
all their sons, headed by Yaugandharāyaṇa,
performed their respective duties for this son of Śatānīka.

3.1.s: evaṃ sa pālayāmāsa mahīṃ rājasuto balī .. 89 ..
3.1.d: एवं स पालयामास महीं राजसुतो बली .. 89 ..
3.1.m: Thus the mighty prince ruled the earth.
As time passed, having been invited by Mahendra to a great festival with his son,
he heard a story of the future spoken by him:
"The heavenly woman Alambuṣā, through the curse of Brahmā, in Ayodhyā
was born as Mṛgāvatī, the daughter of King Kṛtavarman.

3.1.s: vidhūma nāmā ca vasustvaṃ nākalalanāṃ purā ..
3.1.d: विधूम नामा च वसुस्त्वं नाकललनां पुरा ..
3.1.m: And you, a Vasu named Vidhūma, formerly in the abode of Brahmā,
having seen that very celestial woman whose garment was stripped away by the wind,
were overcome with passion at once and came to mortality through a curse.

3.1.s: saiva te dayitā rājanbhāvinī na cirātsakhe .. 93 ..
3.1.d: सैव ते दयिता राजन्भाविनी न चिरात्सखे .. 93 ..
3.1.m: She alone will be your beloved wife before long, O king, my friend!

3.1.s: yadā tvamātmanaḥ putraṃ rājye saṃsthāpya bhūpate ..
3.1.d: यदा त्वमात्मनः पुत्रं राज्ये संस्थाप्य भूपते ..
3.1.m: When, having installed your own son upon the kingdom, O ruler of the earth,
along with your wife Mṛgāvatī, on the shore of the southern ocean,
at the most holy Cakratīrtha near Phullagrāma,
you perform a ritual ablution, then you will be freed from the curse."
Thus spoke the lord Pitāmaha in Satyaloka.
Hearing this speech of Indra, King Sahasrānīka,
filled with longing for the wedding, bade farewell to Śacī's lord,

3.1.s: kauśāṃbīṃ prasthito hṛṣṭaḥ sa tilottamayā pathi .. .. 97 ..
3.1.d: कौशांबीं प्रस्थितो हृष्टः स तिलोत्तमया पथि .. .. 97 ..
3.1.m: and set out joyfully for Kauśāmbī. On the way, as Tilottamā
was speaking to him, his mind was wholly absorbed, remembering that beloved lady;
meditating on the words of Śatakratu, the king did not look at her.
Slighted by the disrespect, that fair-browed maiden cursed the king:
"Even when called by me, O King Sahasrānīka,
why do you neglect me, contemplating Mṛgāvatī in your heart?
Proud women, intoxicated by their beauty and good fortune, do not tolerate disrespect!
Disdaining me, the one whom you now meditate upon in your heart, O king,
separated from her you shall be for fourteen years!"

3.1.s: iti śaptavatīṃ rājā tāmu vāca tilottamām..
3.1.d: इति शप्तवतीं राजा तामु वाच तिलोत्तमाम्..
3.1.m: To Tilottamā who had cursed him thus, the king said:
"If only I obtain her, the daughter of Kṛtavarman,
I will endure for fourteen years the grief born of separation from her!"

3.1.s: ityuktvā tadgatamanā nṛpaḥ prāyā nnijāṃ purīm .. 103 ..
3.1.d: इत्युक्त्वा तद्गतमना नृपः प्राया न्निजां पुरीम् .. 103 ..
3.1.m: Having spoken thus, his mind fixed on her, the king went to his own city.
Then, in the course of time, the daughter of King Kṛtavarman,
that beloved lady who was the all-in-all of the flower-bowed [Kāma], reached him.
Having obtained Mṛgāvatī, a creeping vine upon the tree of amorous sport,
a wave upon the ocean of charm, he, radiant as Kāma, rejoiced.
From him she conceived a child, as Bhavānī did from the moon-crested [Śiva];
with paleness she shone like a crescent of the moon washed with nectar.
Then, with the manifestation of pregnancy-cravings, the beautiful queen shone
like the eastern quarter pregnant with the maker of the night.
Under the influence of her pregnancy-cravings, whatever desire the queen harbored,
though exceedingly hard to attain, he lovingly procured all of it for her.
While her husband was fulfilling every wish, once Mṛgāvatī,
of her own accord, set her mind on bathing in a reservoir of blood.
Learning Mṛgāvatī's desire, the ruler of the earth
in an instant had a pool filled with safflower-dyed water prepared.
In that red water, the queen eagerly performed her bath.
Then, seeing her wet with red water, resembling a blossoming kiṃśuka,
a monstrous bird born of the lineage of Suparṇa,
mistaking the king's wife for raw meat, carried off the charming woman by the power of cruel fate.
Carrying her far away through the sky, that mountain-like [bird]
abandoned her, helpless with fainting, in a cave of the Udaya mountain.
Having slowly regained consciousness, the slender vine of her body trembling with shivers,
she shed tears repeatedly from her eyes that resembled blue lotuses.
"Alas, my lord! Unfortunate am I, tormented by separation from you!

3.1.s: kā gatiḥ kva nu gacchāmi drakṣyāmi tvanmukhaṃ kadā..115..
3.1.d: का गतिः क्व नु गच्छामि द्रक्ष्यामि त्वन्मुखं कदा..115..
3.1.m: What refuge is there? Where indeed shall I go? When will I see your face?"
Having said this, desiring death, she placed herself before elephants and lions;
yet, abandoned by all the lions and elephants, she did not meet her death.

3.1.s: āpatkāle nṛṇāṃ nūnaṃ maraṇaṃ naiva labhyate..
3.1.d: आपत्काले नृणां नूनं मरणं नैव लभ्यते..
3.1.m: In a time of misfortune, death is truly not obtained by human beings.
Hearing her extremely pitiful lamentation, with upturned faces,
the deer, their movements arrested, did not even graze on grass.
Then, seeing her in such a state, the son of a sage, an ocean of compassion,
out of pity brought the weeping queen to his hermitage,
and presented that queen to his teacher Jamadagni.
The righteous Jamadagni consoled her at his side.
Jamadagni said:

3.1.s: tathā jānīhi māṃ bhadre kṛtavarmā yathā tava .. 3.1.5.120 ..
3.1.d: तथा जानीहि मां भद्रे कृतवर्मा यथा तव .. 3.1.5.120 ..
3.1.m: "Know me to be just like your Kṛtavarman, O blessed lady."
Thus consoled there out of compassion by Jamadagni,

3.1.s:
cakre tatraiva sā vāsamāśrame munisaṃkule .. 121 .. .
tatassvalpena kālena viśākhamiva pārvatī ..
3.1.d:
चक्रे तत्रैव सा वासमाश्रमे मुनिसंकुले .. 121 .. .
ततस्स्वल्पेन कालेन विशाखमिव पार्वती ..
3.1.m: she took up residence right there in the hermitage crowded with sages. / Then, in a short time, just as Pārvatī bore Viśākha,
the young woman gave birth to a son endowed with the virtues of valor and fortitude.
Whatever rites of the lying-in chamber ought to be performed by relatives,
the wives of the sages performed them like mothers for Mṛgāvatī.
A bodiless voice [spoke regarding] that well-born son of the king;

Śrī Sūta said:
Because the goddess founded this matchless city in her own name,
therefore this excellent city of the goddess is called Devīpattana.
Starting from Devīpattana on an auspicious day at a favorable hour, O brahmins,
having first bowed to Vighneśvara and likewise to the Lord of the Waters,
permitted by Mahādeva, the exceedingly righteous Rāmacandra,
joyfully establishing the nine stones with his own hand,
began the bridge as far as Laṅkā, unwearied, O brahmins.
Ascending the auspicious throne made by Nala, Rāma
caused the bridge to be built in the ocean by the monkeys led by Nala.
Mountains, branching trees, boulders, piles of timber,
and grasses the monkeys fetched from within the forest.
Taking them, Nala built the bridge across the great ocean.
In five days, reaching to the vicinity of Laṅkā,
ten yojanas broad and a hundred yojanas long,
the bridge was built in the ocean by Nala, holy and destroying sin.
Near Devīpura, at the form of the nine stones,
at the base of the bridge a man should bathe for the purification of his sins.
He should likewise bathe at Cakratīrtha and revere Hari, the Lord of the Bridge.
The construction of the bridge that was made beginning from Devīpattana,
that, O chiefs of brahmins, is considered to be truly the base of the bridge.
The western point of the bridge is celebrated as Darbhaśayyā,
and Devīpurī is the eastern point; both are the base of the bridge.
Both are declared meritorious, purifying, and destroying sin.

3.1.m: Having first bathed at the base of the bridge and likewise at Cakratīrtha,
they should subsequently go to the Setubandha with solemn resolve.
In Devīpura as well as at Darbhaśayyā, O earthly gods,
bathing in the auspicious Cakratīrtha destroys merits and sins.
Just by remembrance of Cakratīrtha in both places, O brahmins,
even sins accumulated over a hundred thousand births turn to ashes.
Birth itself is dissolved, and liberation stands in the palm of the hand.

3.1.m: There is no sacred ford equal to Cakratīrtha, nor will there ever be.
Whatever sacred fords there are on earth, beginning with the Gaṅgā, O best of brahmins,
truly do not equal a sixteenth part of Cakratīrtha.
First, one should bathe in the ocean in the midst of the nine stones;
then one should offer the kṣetrapiṇḍa, and likewise at Cakratīrtha.
One should serve Hari, the Lord of the Bridge, for the purification of one's sins.
Thus should those who have gone by that path do at Darbhaśayyā.
The person who bows to the throne made by Nala,
mounted by Rāmacandra, has no fear of hell.
One should first bow down to the bridge, contemplating Rāma in the heart at that time:
“To the one whose dust is purified by the stepping of the hero of the Raghu race,
to the cause of the severing of the Ten-necked one's heads, to the bridge, homage!
To the banner of Rāmacandra, to the sole cause of the path of liberation,
to the sun for the lotus of Sītā’s mind, to the bridge, homage!”
Having first bowed down with all eight limbs using this mantra, O brahmins,
one should then go to the sacred ford Vetālavarada of great power.
From bathing there, a man attains supreme perfection.

Śrī Sūta said:
Long ago, O twice-born ones, there was a rākṣasa named Kapālābharaṇa. (7)
He had become unslayable by all the gods through a boon from Brahmā.
His excellent minister was named Śavabhakṣaṇa. (8)
He had a hundred akṣauhiṇīs teeming with horses, elephants, and chariots.

3.1.m: He also had a city famed as Vaijayanta. (9)
Dwelling in that city, this mighty Kapālābharaṇa
summoned the minister Śavabhakṣa and spoke, O twice-born ones: (10)
“O Śavabhakṣa of great prowess, skilled in the sciences of counsel,
let us go to the city of the gods, defeat the deities in battle, (11)
and dwell in Śakra's delightful palace along with our troops.
Let us take delight in his Nandana [garden] with hosts of apsarases headed by Rambhā.” (12)
Hearing these words of Kapālābharaṇa at that time,
Śavabhakṣa replied on that matter, O brahmins: “So be it.” (13)
Then the mighty Kapālābharaṇa installed his heroic son
Durmedhas in the city, and surrounded by his army, (14)
set out for Amarāvatī, eager to fight with the immortals,
drying up seas and rivers with the mass of dust raised (15)
by elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers, and crushing even mountains,
and making heaven and earth resound, O brahmins, with the sound of kettle-drums, (16)
with the neighing calls of horses and the trumpeting of elephants,
with the fierce rumblings of chariot wheels and the lion-roars of foot-soldiers. (17)
Making deaf the ears of the elephants of the quarters,
he marched to the city of the gods, desiring to fight with the immortals. (18)
Then Indra and the other gods, hearing the clamorous uproar of the army,
sallied forth from the city, O twice-born ones, their minds bent on battle. (19)
Then a battle took place between the gods and the rākṣasas,
the like of which had never been seen before in the world, nor ever heard of. (20)
Then Indra and the other gods slew the rākṣasas in the fight,
and the rākṣasas, striving for victory, struck down the gods in the fray. (21)
Single combats also broke out mutually between the gods and the rakṣases:
the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra fought in battle against Kapālābharaṇa; (22)
Śavabhakṣa fought with Yama, and Kauśika with Varuṇa;
Kubera fought with Rudhirākṣa, O best of brahmins. (23)
Māṃsapriya, Madyasevin, Krūradṛṣṭi, and Bhayāvaha—
these four valiant younger brothers of Kapālābharaṇa— (24)
fought against each other in battle with the two Aśvins, Agni, and Vāyu.
Then the mighty, swift Yama, with his staff of death, (25)
struck down Śavabhakṣa in battle and sent him to the abode of Yama,
and Yama slaughtered his thirty akṣauhiṇīs in the fray. (26)
In the battle, Varuṇa struck off Kauśika's head with a dart;
Kubera severed Rudhirākṣa's head with a lance. (27)
The younger brothers of Kapālābharaṇa, slain in battle, O brahmins,
by the two Aśvins, Agni, and Vāyu, departed to Yama's abode. (28)
The hundred akṣauhiṇīs, O twice-born ones, slaughtered in battle by the lord of the gods
within half a watch of the day, departed to Yama's abode. (29)

Holy Sītākuṇḍa removes all sins and grants liberation;
it destroys hordes of great sins and is the supreme nectar.
It appeases all sorrows and removes all poverty;
it bestows wealth and grain, is pure, and grants the realm of Vaikuṇṭha and others.
Therefore, O slayer of Vṛtra, perform a sacrifice there at Sītāsaras.”

3.1.m: Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled “Release of Indra from the Sin of Brahmin-slaughter in the Praise of Sītāsaras,” in the Setumāhātmya of the third Brahmakhaṇḍa in the glorious Skandapurāṇa, a collection of eighty-one thousand verses.
The venerable Sūta said:
Having bathed in the greatly holy Sītākuṇḍa, O best of brahmins,
a man should then, with concentrated mind, approach the Maṅgala sacred ford,
where Kamalā [Lakṣmī], beloved of Viṣṇu, is ever present,
and to which lake indeed the gods,
all headed by Śatakratu [Indra], constantly go to ward off misfortune.
Concerning this sacred ford that purifies the worlds, O seers,
I shall narrate a holy story that destroys sins.
Formerly, a king named Manojava, born in the Lunar dynasty,
protected in accordance with righteousness the earth girdled by the oceans.
He worshipped the gods with sacrifices, and the brahmins with mounds of food;
every year he gratified the ancestral gods with sacrificial offerings.
He studied the triple Veda constantly, and recited the treatises with understanding;
he conquered enemies through valor, and bowed down to Śiva and Keśava [Viṣṇu].
He delighted in the manuals of statecraft, and likewise recited the great mantras.

3.1.s: evaṃ sa dharmato rājā pālayāmāsa medinīm ..

3.1.m: In this way, according to righteousness, the king protected the earth.
As he ruled, all obstacles were eradicated from the king's realm.
Arrogance arose in him, which destroys sons and wealth.
Where arrogance is present, there also arise greed and intoxication;

3.1.m: desire, anger, violence, and deluding malice—
these, O best of brahmins, are the causes of the destruction of fortune.

3.1.s: etāni yatra vidyaṃte puruṣe sa vinaśyati ..

3.1.m: In whatever man these are present, he perishes
in an instant, along with his sons, grandsons, and all his wealth.
Malice arose in him, constantly bearing hatred toward people.
His mind agitated by malice, vainly arrogant,
greedy, and corrupted by desire, his mind was turned thus:
He resolved, “I will collect taxes from the villages of the brahmins.”

3.1.m: out of greed, he indeed seized the money and grain of the brahmins.

and of the great-souled vipras, / and of the gods beginning with Śiva and Viṣṇu.
His mind bewildered by egotism, he seized their sacred fields.
When he had thus become unjust, an enemy to gods and twice-born,
by the ripening of his evil deeds, O best of the twice-born, a cruel,
powerful enemy, the ruler of another country, besieged his city.
Equipped with a fourfold army, O chiefs of vipras, [a king] named Golabha—
there was a battle lasting six months with Golabha by the wicked-souled,
arrogance-loving king Manojava.
Then, defeated in battle by Golabha, fallen from his kingdom,
that Manojava went into the forest together with his son and wife.
Golabha remained ruling for a long time in Manojava's city.
Possessed of a fourfold army, having expelled him in battle, the mighty one [remained].
Manojava too, O chiefs of vipras, grieving, accompanied by his wife and son,
emaciated by hunger and constantly stumbling, entered the great forest,
resounding with swarms of crickets, terrifying with tigers and beasts of prey,
filled with the trumpeting of elephants, crowded with boars and buffaloes.
In that most dreadful forest, afflicted by hunger,
the child, Manojava's son, begged his father for food:

3.1.s: aṃba mennaṃ prayaccha tvaṃ kṣudhā māṃ bādhate bhṛśam ..24 ..

Thus, through the abundance of evil deeds, defeated by Golabha,

3.1.m: nor was a reservoir dug, nor a well, nor a pool;
no flower garden was planted, nor a grove of tulasī,

3.1.m: nor was a shrine to Śiva or Viṣṇu built by me, O beloved."
Because of that sin, this suffering has come upon me today.

3.1.s: na mayā paitṛke māsi pitṝnuddiśya śobhane ..

3.1.m: During the ancestral month, O fair lady, for the sake of the ancestors,

How did the name Ekāntarāmanātha come to that sacred field,
O Sūta? You ought to tell this, O sage.
O tiger among sages, our desire to hear that is very great.
The venerable Sūta said:
Formerly, Rāma, son of Daśaratha, along with Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa,
accompanied by his brother Lakṣmaṇa and by Hanūmat who knows counsel,
while the bridge was being built in the midst of the ocean by the monkeys,
thinking of Sītā in his mind, deliberated in secret.
While they were taking counsel concerning the slaying of Rāvaṇa and the others,
the ocean roared intensely, its billowing waves tossing high.
While the terrible, mighty roar of the ocean was resounding,
they could not hear what was spoken to one another.
Then, becoming somewhat enraged, with a glance curved in a frown,
Rāma, having restrained the ocean with playful knit of his brow,
took counsel, O best of brahmins, concerning the destruction of the rākṣasas.
Because Rāghava deliberated there in secret with them,
that sacred field came to be called Ekāntarāmanātha, O brahmins.
This very ocean, restrained by the playful knit of Rāma's brow,
even today is seen with motionless water in those regions.
This is that excellent sacred field named Ekāntarāmanātha.
Having arrived and having bathed in Amṛtavāpī according to the rule,
those who venerate Rāma and the others will all attain liberation.
Though destitute of non-dual knowledge and discernment, lacking detachment and devoid of deep meditation,
and abandoned of rituals such as Vedic sacrifices, having bathed here they will attain immortality, O best of brahmins.

3.1.s: iti śrīskāṃde mahāpurāṇa ekāśītisāhasryāṃ saṃhitāyāṃ tṛtīye brahmakhaṇḍe setumāhātmye amṛtavāpīpraśaṃsāyām agastyabhrātṛvimuktivarṇanaṃnāma trayodaśo'dhyāyaḥ .. 13 ..
3.1.d: इति श्रीस्कांदे महापुराण एकाशीतिसाहस्र्यां संहितायां तृतीये ब्रह्मखण्डे सेतुमाहात्म्ये अमृतवापीप्रशंसायाम् अगस्त्यभ्रातृविमुक्तिवर्णनंनाम त्रयोदशोऽध्यायः .. 13 ..
3.1.m: Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, named 'The Description of the Liberation of Agastya's Brother in Praise of Amṛtavāpī', in the Setumāhātmya of the third Brahmakhaṇḍa in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa of eighty-one thousand verses.
The venerable Sūta said:
Having bathed in Amṛtavāpī and worshipped Ekāntarāghava,

3.1.s: jiteṃdriyo naraḥ snātuṃ brahmakuṃḍaṃ tato vrajet .. 1 ..
3.1.d: जितेंद्रियो नरः स्नातुं ब्रह्मकुंडं ततो व्रजेत् .. 1 ..
3.1.m: a man with subdued senses should then go to Brahmakuṇḍa to bathe.
In the middle of the bridge, on the Gandhamādana mountain,
there is a great sacred ford known as Brahmakuṇḍa, a cure for all poverty;
it destroys tens of millions of murders of a brahmin.
The sight of Brahmakuṇḍa destroys the entire flood of sins.

3.1.s: kiṃ tasya bahubhistīrthaiḥ kiṃ tapobhiḥ kimadhvaraiḥ ..
3.1.d: किं तस्य बहुभिस्तीर्थैः किं तपोभिः किमध्वरैः ..
3.1.m: What need has he of many sacred fords, what need of austerities, what need of sacrifices,
and what need has he of great gifts—he who gazes upon Brahmakuṇḍa?
A single ritual ablution in Brahmakuṇḍa is the cause of attaining Vaikuṇṭha.
He by whom the ash produced from Brahmakuṇḍa is applied, O brahmins,
the three gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara attend upon him.
Whoever makes the tripuṇḍra mark with the ash produced from Brahmakuṇḍa—

3.1.s: karoti tasya kaivalyaṃ karasthaṃ nātra saṃśayaḥ ..
3.1.d: करोति तस्य कैवल्यं करस्थं नात्र संशयः ..
3.1.m: absolute liberation rests in his hand; there is no doubt about this.
Or if even an atom of that ash is borne upon one's forehead,
just by that much his liberation would occur; no doubt is to be entertained here.
That mortal who smears himself with the ash of that kuṇḍa,

3.1.s: tasya puṇyaphalaṃ vaktuṃ śaṃkaro vetti vā na vā ..
3.1.d: तस्य पुण्यफलं वक्तुं शंकरो वेत्ति वा न वा ..
3.1.m: whether Śaṃkara knows how to describe the fruit of his merit or not!
Whoever does not bear the ash produced from Brahmakuṇḍa
will fall into the Raurava hell as long as the moon and stars endure.
That lowest of men who does not apply ash from Brahmakuṇḍa

3.1.s: narādhamo na kuryādyaḥ sukhaṃ nāsya kadācana ..
3.1.d: नराधमो न कुर्याद्यः सुखं नास्य कदाचन ..
3.1.m: as anointment or as a tripuṇḍra mark has never any happiness.
Whoever is devoted to reviling the ash produced from Brahmakuṇḍa,
a wise man should infer illegitimate mixture in his birth.
This ash produced from Brahmakuṇḍa purifies the world;

3.1.s: anyabhasmasamaṃ yastu nyūnaṃ vā vakti mānavaḥ ..
3.1.d: अन्यभस्मसमं यस्तु न्यूनं वा वक्ति मानवः ..
3.1.m: the human being who declares it equal to or less than any other ash,
a wise man must infer confusion of caste in his birth. (13)
Even when this ash originating from the Brahmakuṇḍa is readily available,
the man who applies the tripuṇḍra with any other ash— (14)
a wise man must infer confusion of caste in his birth.

3.1.s: kadācidapi yo martyo bhasmaitattu na dhārayet .. 15 ..
3.1.d: कदाचिदपि यो मर्त्यो भस्मैतत्तु न धारयेत् .. 15 ..
3.1.m: Whatever mortal never applies this ash, (15)
a wise man must infer confusion of caste in his birth.
Whoever gives to a brahmin the ash born from the Brahmakuṇḍa, (16)
by him the earth bounded by the four oceans has been given.
No doubt should be entertained in this matter; I swear it thrice! (17)
It is true, it is true, it is true again; with arm raised it is declared:
Apply the ash originating from the Brahmakuṇḍa, O best of brahmins! (18)
For this purifying ash arose from the sacrifice of Brahmā.
Long ago, indeed, the blessed Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds, (19)
in the presence of all the gods on Mount Gandhamādana,
performed all the sacrificial rites to avert the curse of the Lord. (20)
Having performed in accordance with rule all the sacrifices with generous sacrificial gifts,
Brahmā was swiftly freed from the curse of Śambhu, O best of brahmins! (21)
Those men who, having approached this sacred ford, take their ritual ablution,
they attain union with Mahādeva; there is no doubt. (22)
The seers said:
O disciple of Vyāsa, of great wisdom, skilled in the meaning of the Purāṇas!
Against the creator of the fourteen worlds, the four-faced one, (23)
for what offense did Śambhu curse the husband of Bhāratī?

3.1.s: śāpaśca kīdṛśastasya purā datto hareṇa vai ..
3.1.d: शापश्च कीदृशस्तस्य पुरा दत्तो हरेण वै ..
3.1.m: And what kind of curse was formerly given to him by Hara?
Tell us all this in truth, O sage, out of affection. (24)
The auspicious Sūta said:
Long ago, a quarrel arose mutually between Brahmā and Viṣṇu, (25)
as they praised themselves in rivalry over a certain cause:

3.1.s: ahaṃ karttā na matto'nyaḥ karttāsti jagatītale .. .. 26 ..
3.1.d: अहं कर्त्ता न मत्तोऽन्यः कर्त्तास्ति जगतीतले .. .. 26 ..
3.1.m: “I am the creator; there is no creator other than me on the surface of the earth!” (26)

3.1.s: evamāha hariṃ brahmā brahmāṇaṃ ca haristathā ..
3.1.d: एवमाह हरिं ब्रह्मा ब्रह्माणं च हरिस्तथा ..
3.1.m: Thus Brahmā spoke to Hari, and likewise Hari to Brahmā.
In this way, a very great dispute proceeded between the two in the past. (27)
In the meantime, O brahmins, as the two were quarreling with each other,
to destroy their pride and for the awakening of the two gods, (28)
a liṅga manifested between them, self-luminous and devoid of affliction.

3.1.s: tau dṛṣṭvā vismitau liṃgaṃ brahmaviṣṇu parasparam .. 29 ..
3.1.d: तौ दृष्ट्वा विस्मितौ लिंगं ब्रह्मविष्णु परस्परम् .. 29 ..
3.1.m: Seeing that liṅga, amazed, Brahmā and Viṣṇu mutually (29)
made an agreement, O brahmins, in the presence of the gods in ancient times:
“This great liṅga without beginning or end that is seen before us, (30)
resembling endless suns, equal in radiance to endless fire—
whichever of the two of us shall see the top and bottom of this liṅga, (31)

3.1.s: sa bhavedadhiko loke lokakartā ca sa prabhuḥ ..
3.1.d: स भवेदधिको लोके लोककर्ता च स प्रभुः ..
3.1.m: he shall be superior in the world, the creator of the world, and its lord.
I will go upward, searching for the end of the liṅga; (32)
go down below, O Hari, to search for its base!”

3.1.s: iti tasya vacaḥ śrutvā tathe tyāha ramāpatiḥ .. 33 ..
3.1.d: इति तस्य वचः श्रुत्वा तथे त्याह रमापतिः .. 33 ..
3.1.m: Hearing his words, the husband of Ramā said: “So be it.” (33)

3.1.s: evaṃ tau samayaṃ kṛtvā mārgaṇāya vinirgatau ..
3.1.d: एवं तौ समयं कृत्वा मार्गणाय विनिर्गतौ ..
3.1.m: Having thus made the agreement, the two departed to search.
Viṣṇu, in the form of a boar, went below to search; (34)
the husband of Bhāratī, assuming the nature of a swan, flew upward.
Then Viṣṇu, having searched the lower worlds for many groups of years,
returned to the place and spoke in the presence of the gods. (35)
Viṣṇu said:
“I did not see the beginning of this liṅga,” speaking the truth. (36)
Having searched upward, Brahmā also came there;

3.1.s: āgatya ca vacaḥ prāha chadmanā caturānanaḥ .. .. 37 ..
3.1.d: आगत्य च वचः प्राह छद्मना चतुराननः .. .. 37 ..
3.1.m: and having arrived, the four-faced one uttered a deceitful statement: (37)
Brahmā said:
“I saw the end of this liṅga”—falsely indeed.
Hearing that statement of the two, Brahmā and Viṣṇu, Maheśvara
laughed and spoke thus to the four-faced one who spoke falsely: (38)
Īśvara said:
“Because you spoke an untruth in front of me, O four-faced one, (39)

3.1.s: tasmātpūjā na te bhūyālloke sarvatra sarvadā ..
3.1.d: तस्मात्पूजा न ते भूयाल्लोके सर्वत्र सर्वदा ..
3.1.m: therefore let there be no worship of you in the world, anywhere, at any time!”
Then the blessed Parameśvara spoke again to Viṣṇu: (40)
"Because you spoke the truth, O Hari, lord of Kamalā,

3.1.s: tasmātte matsamā pūjā bhaviṣyati na saṃśayaḥ .. 41 ..
3.1.d: तस्मात्ते मत्समा पूजा भविष्यति न संशयः .. 41 ..
3.1.m: therefore your worship shall be equal to mine, there is no doubt."
Then Brahmā, dejected, spoke to Śaṃkara:
"O Lord, treasure-house of compassion, forgive my offense!
One offense ought to be forgiven by masters, lords of the universe."
Then Maheśvara spoke, consoling Brahmā:
Īśvara said:

3.1.s: na mithyāvacanaṃ me syādbrahmanvakṣyāmi te śṛṇu ..
3.1.d: न मिथ्यावचनं मे स्याद्ब्रह्मन्वक्ष्यामि ते शृणु ..
3.1.m: "My words cannot be false, O Brahmā; listen to what I will tell you:
Go quickly, my child, to Mount Gandhamādana;
perform sacrifices there for the pacification of the fault of lying.
Then, your sin washed away, you will be [restored], there is no doubt.

3.1.s: tena śrauteṣu te brahmansmārteṣvapi ca karmasu ..
3.1.d: तेन श्रौतेषु ते ब्रह्मन्स्मार्तेष्वपि च कर्मसु ..
3.1.m: By virtue of that, O Brahmā, in Vedic and also in domestic rites,

3.1.s: pūjā bhaviṣyati sadā na pūjā pratimāsu te..46..
3.1.d: पूजा भविष्यति सदा न पूजा प्रतिमासु ते..46..
3.1.m: there will always be worship for you, but there will be no worship for you in images."
Having spoken thus, the divine Lord disappeared right there.
Then Brahmā went to Mount Gandhamādana, O brahmins,
and with sacrifices worshipped the creator of sacrifices, the lord of Pārvatī,
for eighty-eight thousand years, O best of sages,
with all the sacrifices such as the Pauṇḍarīka, with bountiful priestly fees;
in the presence of Indra and all the gods, he sacrificed to Śiva.
Gratified by this, Śambhu granted him a boon:
Īśvara said:
"Your fault of false speech has been destroyed here by performing these sacrifices;
O four-faced one, in Vedic and domestic rites,
your spotless worship will take place, O Brahmā, but there will be no worship for you in images.
This sacrificial place of yours will from this day attain fame as 'Brahmakuṇḍa'
in this threefold world, holy and destroying sin.
Whoever performs a ritual ablution even once in the sacred ford named Brahmakuṇḍa,
for him the bolt of the door of liberation is broken at that very moment, O Brahmā.
Applying to his forehead the sacred ash produced from Brahmakuṇḍa,
breaking open the door-leaf of illusion, one will go to the door of liberation.

3.1.s: brahmakuṇḍotthitaṃ bhasma lalāṭe yo na dhārayet ..
3.1.d: ब्रह्मकुण्डोत्थितं भस्म ललाटे यो न धारयेत् ..
3.1.m: He who does not apply to his forehead the sacred ash arisen from Brahmakuṇḍa
is not a son born of his father's seed in his mother.
From applying the sacred ash produced from Brahmakuṇḍa, O Brahmā,
ten thousand murders of a brahmin are destroyed, as well as ten thousand drinkings of liquor;
ten thousand defilements of the guru's bed are destroyed, as well as ten thousand thefts of gold;
ten thousand associations with them are destroyed; I have spoken the truth, O Brahmā.
By the power of applying the sacred ash produced from Brahmakuṇḍa,
bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and other spirits perish in a mere moment."
Having spoken thus, the divine Lord disappeared right there.
When the sacrifices were completed, the sages of subdued senses,
the gods headed by Indra, along with siddhas, cāraṇas, and kinnaras,
and other hosts of gods on Mount Gandhamādana,
resorting to that sacrificial ground attended by Rudra himself,
remained there continually, knowing its glory.
Then Brahmā, having completed the sacrifices with plentiful priestly fees according to rule,
went to Satyaloka, having obtained his wish from Śiva.

3.1.m: From that time forward, the gods, sages, and best of brahmins, / coming to Brahmakuṇḍa, performed sacrifices according to the ordinances. / Therefore, mortals wishing to sacrifice should perform sacrifices right here. / Revered by humans, gods, and lords of sages, bringing an end to all transmigratory existence, O brahmins, / this auspicious pool of the lotus-born [Brahmā] takes away all sin and grants all desired aims. / Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, named 'The Description of the Release from Brahmā's Curse, in the Praise of Brahmakuṇḍa', in the Setumāhātmya of the Brahmakhaṇḍa in the glorious Skandapurāṇa, a collection of eighty-one thousand verses.

3.1.m: Glorious Sūta said: / Having performed a ritual ablution with a concentrated mind in the highly sacred Brahmakuṇḍa, / a man should then go to the pool of Hanūmat, O best of brahmins. / Formerly, when the demons had been slain, when the task of battle was over, / and Rāma and the others had returned to Mount Gandhamādana, / for the benefit of all the worlds, Hanūmat, the son of the Wind, / created the best of all sacred fords bearing his own name. / Knowing the glory of which it is served by Rudra himself, / equal to that sacred ford there has never been, nor will there ever be. / Bathing in which men go to the eternal world of Śiva; / in which highly sacred ford, which destroys great sins, / created by the son of the Wind for the benefit of all worlds, / all the hells became utterly empty for a long time indeed. / Śaṃkara knows the glory of that sacred ford, or perhaps he does not! / Where formerly a king of the Kekaya lineage named Dharmasakha, / having bathed with devotion, obtained one hundred sons. / The seers said: / O Sūta, you ought to tell today the life-story of Dharmasakha, / who, having bathed in the sacred ford of Hanūmatkuṇḍa, obtained one hundred sons. / Glorious Sūta said: / Listen, O seers, to the deeds of that protector of the earth; / today I will relate in brief [the story] of Dharmasakha. / Formerly there was a king named Dharmasakha who had conquered his enemies, was exceedingly righteous, / virtuous, and devoted to the protection of his subjects. / He had one hundred wives, O brahmins, to whom their husband was a deity. / Ruling the earth along with its mountains, forests, and groves, / the king did not obtain in those wives a son to continue his lineage. / Then, for the sake of a son, that protector of the earth made many efforts;

3.1.m:
and for the sake of a son, that ruler of the earth made great gifts.
With sacrifices such as the horse sacrifice, he sacrificed to the gods;
he repeatedly bestowed gifts, foremost of which was the balance-scale gift of a man's weight in gold.
Until midnight, to everyone without restriction,
the ruler of the earth gave food with abundant soup and rich in grain.
He also performed ancestral rites according to rule, directed towards the ancestors;
with senses restrained, he muttered mantras that bestow offspring.
The king performed many such righteous acts for the sake of a son.
Constantly performing unmatched righteous acts with a view toward [getting] a son,
with the passage of a long time, the king reached old age.
Once, as that aged king was thus striving,
a delightful son named Sucandra was born to his eldest wife.
When the son was born, all the mothers, free from jealousy,
noble as they were, raised him equally with milk and other foods.
And to the king, to all the mothers, to the citizens, and to the ministers,

3.1.m:
this son became the cause of joy to their minds and eyes.
Fondling his son, the king attained the highest joy.
Once, while that son was lying in a cradle,
a scorpion stung him on the foot with its tail blazing with poisonous fire.
From the scorpion's sting, the child cried bitterly.
Then all his mothers began to weep, overcome with grief.
Surrounding the boy, O brahmins, a tumultuous uproar arose.
King Dharmasakha then heard that cry of distress,
as he sat in the midst of the assembly with his ministers and royal priest.
Then the king dispatched a chamberlain to find out.
That chamberlain, going up to the outer gate of the inner apartments,
summoned the elderly eunuchs and spoke these words:
“O eunuchs, why are the women of the inner apartments weeping now?
Go there and find out the cause of their crying.
For this purpose the king sent me from the royal assembly.”
Addressed thus, they ascertained the cause of the crying,

Having heard the words of the eunuchs, the chamberlain went to the assembly
and reported to the king that his son had been stung by a scorpion.
Then King Dharmasakha, having heard such an account,
rose up in haste together with his ministers and priest.
Entering the inner apartments along with sorcerers skilled in removing poison,
he had his son treated repeatedly with medicines and the like.
Then, having fondled his son once he regained health,
and having honored the knowers of mantras with gems, gold, and pearls,
the king came out of the inner apartments, deeply agitated by anxiety,
and sat down in that assembly together with his officiating priests, royal priest, and ministers.
There King Dharmasakha, seated upon an excellent throne,
addressed these fitting words to the officiating priests and the royal priest:
Dharmasakha said:
“Having only one son leads only to grief, O best of brahmins!
Childlessness is surely better for men than having an only son.

3.1.m:
Because of constantly being subject to danger, childlessness is indeed better.
Having reflected on this, O brahmins, I married a hundred wives.
And old age has overtaken me along with my wives, O twice-born.
My life-breaths and those of my wives are anchored in this one son.
Upon his death, the death of all my wives is certain.
My own life would also end upon the death of this only son.
Therefore, by what means can I have many sons?
Tell me that means, O brahmins, foremost among knowers of the Veda!
So that I may have a virtuous son with each of my hundred wives,
tell me that rite, looking into the sacred texts according to dharma.
Whether by a great rite or a small one, or even by one difficult to perform,
if that fruit is achievable, I will perform it without doubt.
I will perform the rite prescribed by you, there is no doubt.
Know it as already done; I swear by my merits!
If there is such a rite by which a hundred sons may be obtained,

tell me now where that rite must be performed by me.”
Questioned thus at that time by the king, the officiating priests with the royal priest,
having assembled together, spoke this to the king with complete certainty:
The officiating priests said:
“There is [such a means], O king; we will tell you how a hundred sons
may be born to you from your hundred wives through a great dharma, O king of the Kaikayas.
There is a most holy mountain named Gandhamādana,
which exists in the form of a bridge in the midst of the southern ocean.
crowded with hosts of Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and celestial seers,
destroying great sins of men merely by being seen or touched.
There is a pool there known in the worlds as Hanumatkuṇḍa,
which relieves great sorrow and grants the fruits of heaven and liberation,
which calms the torments of hell, relieves poverty likewise,
gives sons to the sonless, and gives wives to wifeless men.
There, having bathed with self-restraint, that which grants all desired things,
perform with a concentrated mind the sacrifice for getting sons on its bank.

Thus addressed by the brahmins, the officiating priests, together with the family priest,
the king that very moment, [accompanied] by the officiating priests, his wives, and the family priest,
surrounded by ministers and attendants, equipped with the provisions for the sacrifice,
set out for Mount Gandhamādana in the southern ocean.
Having reached Hanumatkuṇḍa, he bathed there together with his army;
he dwelt on its bank for just a month, regularly performing ritual ablutions.
Then, when spring arrived in the month of Caitra, that best of kings,
accompanied by his family priest, began the sacrifice for sons there.
Those officiating priests along with the family priest properly performed the rites
for the royal seer Dharmasakha together with his wives.
When his sacrifice was completed on the bank of Hanūmatkuṇḍa,
the family priest made the king’s wives consume the remnants of the oblation.

He gave innumerable and abundant gifts to the officiating priests,
and the king granted villages to the brahmins, O best of the twice-born.
Accompanied by his ministers, his retinue, and his wives, that righteous
king returned, rejoiced, back to his own city.
Then, after some time had passed, indeed in the tenth month,
the hundred wives gave birth to one hundred most virtuous sons.
Then with a delighted heart, the heroic and great king Dharmasakha,
bathed and purified, having made the resolve, performed the birth-rite at that time.
He gave many cows, lands, sesame seeds, gold, and other gifts to the brahmins.
The senior wife had two sons: an elder and a younger at that time.
All the sons grew up—one hundred and one, O twice-born.
When they had reached maturity, that king, having divided the kingdom among them
and given it [to them], went with his wives to the bridge at Gandhamādana.
Having reached Hanumatkuṇḍa, he practiced austerity on its bank.

A long time passed for that king while he was practicing austerity,
for King Dharmasakha meditating upon the Bearer of the Trident.
Then, when a great amount of time had passed, King Dharmasakha,
righteous and tranquil in mind, went to the law of time there.
The wives of that royal seer also followed their husband at that time.
The eldest son Sucandra too, having performed the funeral rites for his father,
performed the ceremonies up to the ancestral rite with faith.
Because of death here, the king along with his wives went to Vaikuṇṭha.
All those immensely glorious princes, headed by Sucandra,
brothers devoid of envy, enjoyed each their own kingdom.
Thus has the glory of Hanūmatkuṇḍa been told to you, O brahmins,
as well as the most wonderful deeds of King Dharmasakha.
Therefore, for the attainment of all desires, one should bathe in the pool of Hanumat.

3.1.m: Having bathed in the pool of Hanumat, which is frequented by Rudra himself,
one should then go, concentrated in mind, to the Agastitīrtha, O foremost of brahmins.
This sacred ford was fashioned directly by the Pitcher-Born [Agastya],
long ago when a quarrel was taking place between Meru and Vindhya.
Mount Vindhya grew, obstructing the expanse of the world.
Then, when all living beings were breathless, the gods,
having gone to Mount Kailāsa, made this known to Śambhu.
Then he, eager with desire to take Pārvatī's hand in marriage,
having sent Vasiṣṭha and other sages to ask for Pārvatī,
commanded him, "O pot-born one, you must restrain the Vindhya mountain!"

will show you my wedding attire in the most holy Vedāraṇya, without a doubt.
Therefore, go quickly, O chief of sages, to restrain the Vindhya mountain."
Having been spoken to thus, Agastya then subdued the Vindhya mountain, and,
making the surface of the earth level by merely treading upon it with his feet,
having traversed the southern regions, he reached Gandhamādana.

3.1.m: I shall tell that story to you: listen to it, O chiefs of sages!
There is an exceedingly righteous sage named Dīrghatamas;
he had a son renowned as Kakṣīvat.
Invested with the sacred thread, that Kakṣīvat was a celibate student, master of his senses;
he took up residence in the family of his guru to study the Vedas.
Residing in the house of the guru Udaṅka, the son of Dīrghatamas
studied the four Vedas along with their auxiliary branches, and likewise the six treatises,
the epics, the Purāṇas, and also the Upaniṣads.
Having lived for sixty years in the presence of his guru, Kakṣīvat,
about to depart for his own home, O brahmins, gave the sacrificial fee to his guru.
The learned Kakṣīvat, the foremost knower of Brahman, said to the guru:
Kakṣīvat said:
"I am going home, O great sage; grant me permission.
Looking upon me with a glance of compassion, protect me now, O Udaṅka."
Delighted indeed, Udaṅka then said to Kakṣīvat:
Udaṅka said:
"I permit you, O Kakṣīvat; go to your own home.
I shall tell you a means for your marriage, my child: listen to it.
Go to the bridge of Rāma, to Mount Gandhamādana.
There is a sacred ford made by Agastya, bestowing all desires,
granting enjoyment and liberation to men, destroying all sins.
Bathe there, in that source of all auspiciousness;
dwell there for three years, observant of rules and proper conduct.

Renowned as Kakṣīvat, he will become your son-in-law.”
Having spoken thus, the sage Nārada departed by way of the sky.
Svanaya, having heard those words spoken by Nārada,
longed day and night for the arrival of such a one.
“Therefore, gentle and fortunate Kakṣīvat, young ascetic,
go in haste today to Agastyatīrtha to bathe.
Attainment of all auspiciousness will be yours, without a doubt.”
Thus addressed by Udaṅka, the eminent twice-born Kakṣīvat,
permitted by his guru, set forth to Gandhamādana.
Having reached Agastyatīrtha, he bathed there, his senses restrained.
The lordly sage observed a fast at the sacred field for one day.
On the next day, having bathed again, the brahmin broke his fast.
At night Kakṣīvat, dedicated to righteousness, slept right there.

Having mounted that four-tusked elephant resembling the silver mountain,

Śrī Sūta said:
Having performed ritual ablution in this sacred ford of the jar-born [Agastya], a man
should then go to the holy Rāma-kuṇḍa for the sake of release from sin.
The pool of Raghunātha is holy, O twice-born ones, and destroys sin.
A sacrifice performed on the bank of Raghunātha's pool with small sacrificial gifts
yields complete fruit, as do recitation of the Veda and silent prayers.
Even a mere fistful given on the bank of Raghunātha's pool, O twice-born ones,
if bestowed upon a knower of the Veda, becomes multiplied infinitely.
Regarding the Rāmatīrtha, I shall tell, O best of sages,
a most holy narrative that destroys all sins.
An eminent brahmin named Sutīkṣṇa, a sage with restrained mind,
a disciple of Agastya and meditator on the lotus feet of Rāma,
performed very severe austerity on the bank of the pool of Rāmacandra,
reciting the six-syllabled mantra of which Rāmacandra is the presiding deity.
Unwearied, he recited five thousand times every day this king of mantras;
he recited while performing ritual ablutions in the waters of the pool of Raghunātha,
eating begged food, eating in moderation, with anger conquered and the senses controlled.
In this manner, O best of brahmins, Sutīkṣṇa spent a long time.

3.1.m: Then once that sage, constantly meditating on Rāma in his heart,
praised Rāmacandra accompanied by Sītā with devotion.
Sutīkṣṇa said:
Salutations to You, Lord of Janaka’s daughter! Salutations to You, beloved of Hanumat!
Salutations to You, consecrated to protect the sacrifice of the sage Kauśika!
Salutations to You, son of Kausalyā, and dear one of Viśvāmitra!
Salutations to You, breaker of Hara’s bow, served by the immortals,
slayer of Mārīca, sovereign king, destroyer of the life of Tāṭakā!
O foe of Kabandha, O Hari, son of Daśaratha, salutations to You!
Salutations to You, vanquisher of Jāmadagnya! Salutations to the destroyer of Khara!
Salutations to the master of Sugrīva! Salutations to You, slayer of Vālin,
dispeller of the fear and affliction of Vibhīṣaṇa, remover of impurity!
Destroyer of the sorrow of Ahalyā, salutations to You, elder brother of Bharata!
Homage to the destroyer of the ocean's pride, who built a bridge across it! 15
Homage to you, the saving Brahman, homage to you, elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa!
Homage to you, slayer of demons, crusher of Rāvaṇa! 16
To you, bearer of the bow Kodaṇḍa, provider of all protection!
Praising Rāma daily in this manner, that sage Sutīkṣṇa 17
spent his time unceasingly, his intellect fixed on Rāmacandra.
As he was thus repeating the six-syllable mantra of Rāma, 18
and praising Rāmacandra with this hymn of praise, O you of noble vows,
and taking his ritual ablution daily in the sacred ford of Raghunātha, 19
unwavering, exceedingly pure devotion to Rāmacandra arose [in him].
Non-dual knowledge arose, characterised solely by the inner Self; 20
knowledge of the three Vedas without studying [them], and likewise understanding of what had not been heard;
and capacity to enter into another's body arose, O twice-born; 21
the power to travel through the sky, and skill in the arts;
thorough knowledge of treatises unheard, without a teacher; 22
movement through all the worlds without impediment;
the sight of objects beyond the senses, and conversation with the gods; 23
and knowledge of the affairs even of ants and other creatures, O twice-born;
movement likewise into the worlds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahādeva; 24
and independent movement throughout the fourteen worlds.
All these and other [powers], attainable by yogins, O best of men, 25
belonged to Sutīkṣṇa, O brahmins, through his devotion to the sacred ford of Rāma.
Such is the power of that sacred ford: destroying heinous sins, 26
granting great supernatural perfections, meritorious, destroying untimely death,
bestowing enjoyment and liberation to mortals, destroying the suffering of hell, 27
ever bestowing devotion to Rāma, the cause of cutting off transmigration.
Having installed a great liṅga on its bank, the best of the Raghus 28
worshipped that liṅga out of a desire to show grace to the world.
Having bathed in that highly meritorious sacred ford of Rāma, through the sight of that liṅga 29
liberation itself comes to men, to say nothing of other glorious powers.

a bodiless voice then addressed the delight of Dharma:
"O son of Dharma, highly fortunate one, affectionate even to enemies!
Do not undergo the royal consecration; you are not fit for the protection of the kingdom,

caused him who had laid down his weapon to be killed in battle, O king, shamelessly.
Therefore, an abundance of sin exists in you, O delight of Dharma.
Without performing an expiation for this, in the duty of protecting the kingdom

Having spoken thus, that bodiless voice then ceased.

3.1.m: "Do not be afraid, O king; I tell you a means.
Having heard it, let it be performed by you for the pacification of this sin."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"What is that? Tell me, O great yogin, son of Parāśara, treasure of compassion!"
Tell me that now, by which the destruction of my sin may take place without delay.”
Vyāsa said:
“In the southern ocean, on the bridge, on Mount Gandhamādana,
on Rāma’s Bridge, O great king, is that known as Rāmatīrtha.
There is a holy, accomplished lake, the destroyer of great sins,
By the mere sight of which millions of great sins
Go to destruction immediately, just like darkness at the rising of the sun.
When one beholds Rāmatīrtha, fashioned by Rāma himself,
At that very moment he is freed from the slaying of a brahmin; there is no doubt here.
Going there, O great king, to Rāmatīrtha, the bestower of liberation,
Bathe! There will be purification of your sin, and also fitness for the protection of the kingdom.
Make a gift of cows, land, sesame seeds, and garments upon its shore,
and make a gift of gold and silver, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Certainly, purification from these sins will come to you before long.”
Śrī Sūta said:
Addressed thus by Vyāsa, O best of the twice-born, this son of Dharma,
accompanied by Dhaumya at that very moment, along with his younger brothers,
having established Sahadeva in the kingdom, the son of Dharma then
set out on foot, aiming for Rāma’s Bridge.
In only a few days, he went to Rāma’s Bridge.
Having reached Rāmatīrtha together with Dhaumya, the Pāṇḍava,
having made the ritual intention according to rule by the method spoken by his family priest,
bathed in the sacred Rāmasaras sacred ford, which destroys sin.
Having bathed, sipped water, purified his mind, and offered the funeral ball of the sacred field,
that Yudhiṣṭhira bestowed all the gifts spoken by Vyāsa.

3.1.m: “O King Yudhiṣṭhira, all your sin has gone to destruction!
Whatever fault arose for you previously through the slaughter of your teacher
by speaking an untruth through deceit, that too has been destroyed, O scorcher of foes!
Go to your own city, O King, and having gone, protect the earth.
Consecrate yourself; you possess fitness for the protection of the kingdom.”
Having spoken thus, that bodiless voice then fell silent.
Then, delighted, the son of Dharma turned toward that direction,
and having bowed down to that bodiless voice, accompanied by his younger brothers,
he departed for Hāstinapura with an exceedingly joyful heart.
Then, consecrated in the kingship, he protected the earth.
Thus, O brahmins, through plunging into Rāmatīrtha,
the son of Dharma, his sin gone and mind purified, became worthy to protect the kingdom.

Śrī Sūta said:

Indeed, through bathing in Lakṣmaṇatīrtha, all poverty is destroyed,
and to him a long-lived, virtuous, and learned son is born.

“If I render assistance to the Kuru king, (10)

meritorious, purifying, sin-destroying, and a cleanser of the sin of killing a brahmin and the like.
Whoever recites this chapter or hears it with concentrated mind,
he attains liberation free from return, O chiefs of brahmins.

Śrī Sūta said:
Having bathed in the great sacred ford of Lakṣmaṇa, which destroys the sin of killing a brahmin,
one should then go to Jaṭātīrtha for the purification of one's own mind.
For those whose minds are distressed by saṃsāra, overcome with birth, death, and old age,
there is nothing that destroys ignorance other than Jaṭātīrtha, O twice-born ones.
Certain seekers of liberation in the world, desiring purification of the mind,
read the Vedāntas aloud; they do not experience [the truth] in silence.
In the ocean of Vedānta, where the prima facie view is a great crocodile and which swarms with the fish of established conclusions,
fallen here, the ignorant become bewildered, O twice-born ones.
Those who study the Vedāntas at first for the purification of the mind,

Formerly, for the welfare of all, this sacred ford that destroys ignorance

3.1.m: When Rāvaṇa was slain, O brahmins, the righteous Rāma
washed his matted hair in that water; hence it is called Jaṭātīrtha.
Submersion in the water of the Jāhnavī for sixty thousand years,
a single ritual ablution in the Godāvarī when Bṛhaspati is in Leo,
and as many thousands of ritual ablutions in the Gomatī when the teacher of the gods enters Leo,
over [so many] years, is attained through the mere darśana of Jaṭātīrtha.
For men who have bathed in Jaṭātīrtha, O best of the twice-born,
there is purification of the inner organ, and from that, ignorance is destroyed.
Upon the destruction of ignorance, knowledge arises; from that you will attain liberation;
thereafter one becomes filled with undivided existence, consciousness, and bliss.
In this regard also, they cite this ancient history.

by this one crosses difficulties and attains meritorious worlds. (26)

‘O Bhṛgu, on the holy bridge of Rāma, on Mount Gandhamādana, (31)

3.1.m: by merely bathing in Jaṭātīrtha, purity of intellect certainly comes to be.’
He, Bhṛgu, son of Varuṇa, at once by his father's word, (32)
went and bathed in Jaṭātīrtha, and obtained purity of intellect.
With the continuous series of his ignorance destroyed by that purity then, Bhṛgu, (33)
having developed the realization of non-duality from his own father Varuṇa,
became one whose form is full of undivided being-consciousness-bliss, O Śuka. (34)
Durvāsas too, a portion of Śaṃkara, through the ablution at Jaṭātīrtha,
swiftly attained mental purity and became filled with the bliss of Brahman. (35)
Dattātreya too, a portion of Viṣṇu, by bathing in this sacred ford,
with his internal organ purified, took on the form of Brahman, O Śuka. (36)
Whoever desires the destruction of ignorance should bathe in that which is named Jaṭā,
the purest, meritorious sacred ford that destroys all sins. (37)
Therefore, O wise Śuka, go to Jaṭātīrtha too,
and take a bath in that merit-giving [waters], which bestows purity of mind.” (38)
Having been told thus by his father Vyāsa then, O brahmins, his son Śuka (39)
to the highly meritorious bridge of Rāma, to Mount Gandhamādana,
went, desiring to bathe in Jaṭātīrtha, which bestows supreme purity.

Whatever desire aiming at which, O best of brahmins,

It dispels severe poverty, bestows great abundance of grain,

Having bathed here, Dharmaputra attained great sovereignty,
formerly while dwelling in Indraprastha, urged by glorious Kṛṣṇa. // 4
The seers said:
How Dharmaputra attained sovereignty from plunging into Lakṣmītīrtha
by Kṛṣṇa's instruction, tell us that, O great sage! // 5
Glorious Sūta said:
In Indraprastha of old, O brahmins, directed by Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
the five Pāṇḍavas dwelt, possessing great strength and prowess. // 6
At one time Kṛṣṇa went to Indraprastha to see them.
Beholding him arrived, those Pāṇḍavas, eagerly expectant, // 7
brought him to their home, filled with supreme joy.
That Kṛṣṇa lived there for some time in that best of cities. // 8
Once Yudhiṣṭhira, having called Kṛṣṇa and worshipped him,
asked the lotus-eyed Vāsudeva, lord of the world: // 9
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O deeply wise one! By which virtue do human beings
attain great sovereignty? Tell us that, O wise one!
Thus addressed by the son of Dharma, Kṛṣṇa spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira. // 10
Glorious Kṛṣṇa said:
O son of Dharma, highly fortunate one, on Mount Gandhamādana // 11

3.1.m: Having bathed in this holy sacred ford, Kubera, whose vehicle is a man,
became the master of the treasures, foremost among which is the Mahāpadma.
Therefore you too, O king of kings, at the auspicious Lakṣmītīrtha,
having bathed surrounded by your younger brothers headed by Vṛkodara,

3.1.m: will obtain great fortune and also conquer your enemies.
No doubt should be entertained here, O son of my father's sister, born of Dharma.
Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa, this son of Dharma, of wondrous sight,
went quickly with his younger brothers to Mount Gandhamādana.
Having then gone to Lakṣmītīrtha, the cause of great sovereignty,
Yudhiṣṭhira bathed there with his younger brothers, observing vows.
In the water of Lakṣmītīrtha, which destroys all sins,
he bathed with his younger brothers for one month according to the rules.
He gave many cows, lands, sesamum seeds, gold, and other gifts to brahmins.
Then that son of Dharma went with his younger brothers to Indraprastha.
Yudhiṣṭhira then desired to perform the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Wishing to sacrifice, the son of Dharma summoned Kṛṣṇa.
Kṛṣṇa, summoned in haste by the messenger of the son of Dharma,
mounted a swift chariot yoked with four horses,
and, accompanied by Satyabhāmā, arrived at Indraprastha.
Seeing him arrive, the son of Dharma, out of great joy,
then disclosed to Kṛṣṇa his undertaking of the Rājasūya.
Kṛṣṇa also assented, saying, “Let it be done precisely so.”
And he spoke words full of reason to the son of Dharma:
“O son of my father's sister, O righteous-souled one, listen to my beneficial words.
This Rājasūya is difficult to perform even for all lords of the earth.
Possessing many hundreds of foot-soldiers, chariots, elephants, and horses,
such a ruler of the earth is fit to perform this sacrifice, none other.

Having summoned his four brothers, the son of Dharma spoke, gladdening them:
“O Bhīma of mighty arms! O Dhanañjaya of great prowess!
And you two twins of delicate limbs, consecrated for the destruction of enemies!

3.1.m: And that must be performed after conquering all the lords of the earth in battle.
Therefore, all four of you, accompanied by troops, to conquer the kings,
go to the four quarters, you who are exceedingly heroic.
With the wealth brought by you, I shall perform the great sacrifice.”
Thus respectfully addressed, all the younger brothers of the son of Dharma,
headed by Vṛkodara, becoming cheerful-faced, from the city
the Pāṇḍavas set out in all directions for the conquest of kings.
Having conquered all the many kings situated in the four directions,
bringing those rulers of men under their control, the sons of Pāṇḍu,
taking the manifold, countless, and unsurpassed wealth given by them,
relying upon Kṛṣṇa, swiftly returned to their own city.
Bhīma of great strength and valor arrived there
at the excellent city, having collected a hundred bhāras of gold.
Then Arjuna, having taken a thousand bhāras of gold,

endowed with great splendor, returned to the excellent city of Śakraprastha.

and seizing the accumulation of wealth of the southern kings,

of gold coins did Kṛṣṇa, the Yādava, give to Dharmaputra.
With such immeasurable vast treasures brought by his younger brothers,
and also with the immeasurable wealth given by Kṛṣṇa, Yudhiṣṭhira,
the Pāṇḍava, taking refuge in Kṛṣṇa, performed the Rājasūya sacrifice, O brahmins.
In that sacrifice, he gave wealth to the brahmins to their heart's content.

By however much gold and the like the petitioners were satisfied,
the son of Dharma caused double that amount to be given to them.
So much varied wealth was given to the petitioners
that ten million Brahmās were not able to measure its extent.
Seeing the riches being given away to the petitioners there,
the people truly said: “Ah, all his property has been given by the king!”
Then, seeing the endless treasuries with their infinite jewels and gold,
the people said: “Very little indeed has been given to the petitioners!”
Having thus sacrificed with the Rājasūya, Dharmaputra, along with his younger brothers,
abounding in great wealth, rejoiced in that excellent city.
Through the māhātmya of Lakṣmītīrtha, Dharmaputra Yudhiṣṭhira

3.1.m: obtained all this, O brahmins. Ah, the grandeur of the sacred ford!
This sacred ford is greatly meritorious, destroying great poverty;
it bestows wealth and grain upon men, and destroys great sins.
It annihilates great hells and averts great sorrows.
It bestows liberation and heaven constantly, freeing from great debts;
it gives men a good wife, and it gives good sons.
